rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No. The AI system is high-risk under the AI Act; "medium risk" is a device-classification label under the Medical Device Regulation and has no counterpart in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, which does not operate a graded scale for this route. The classification follows Article 6(1), which treats an AI system as high-risk where two cumulative conditions are met: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; and (b) that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service under that same legislation. The operator's facts satisfy both limbs: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices is listed in Annex I, point 11 (Section A), and the device is subject to a notified-body assessment. Article 6(1) applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the device it serves, so supplying the component separately does not change the outcome. The trigger in Article 6(1)(b) is binary: it asks only whether third-party assessment is required, not how demanding it is. The device's MDR risk class is therefore relevant only as the reason a notified body is involved at all; it does not carry across as a proportionate AI Act risk grade. A lower MDR class that permitted full self-certification would take the system out of Article 6(1)(b) altogether, it would not make it a lesser-risk AI system. Nor is there a route to de-classify it. The derogation in Article 6(3), narrow procedural task, improvement of a previously completed human activity, detection of decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or a preparatory task, and in each case no significant risk of harm, with profiling of natural persons always defeating the derogation, is expressly available only "by derogation from paragraph 2", i.e. only to Annex III systems, together with the documented self-assessment under Article 6(4). It has no application to an Annex I safety component. Equally, Article 7 concerns Commission delegated acts amending the Annex III list and does not bear on the operator's classification. In consequence, the system must meet the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements (Articles 8 to 15), including the documented, iterative lifecycle risk-management system under identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights, estimation and evaluation of risks under the intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of post-market monitoring data, adoption of targeted risk-management measures with due consideration of their combined effects and interactions under Article 9(4), testing under Article 9(5), and acceptable residual risks per hazard and overall, communicated to the deployer under Article 9(6). Article 8(2) lets you integrate the necessary testing, reporting, information and documentation into the procedures already required under the MDR, and in practice Article 9 maps onto the ISO 14971 hazard-identification, risk-estimation and risk-evaluation cycle you already run. Conformity assessment runs through Article 43(3), not Annex VI or Annex VII as standalone procedures: you follow the MDR procedure, the Section 2 requirements form part of that assessment, and points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII apply in addition, notified-body examination of the Annex IV technical documentation, with access where relevant to training, validation and testing datasets, power to require further evidence or tests or to conduct tests itself, and, as a last resort on reasoned request, access to the training and trained models including relevant parameters, subject to intellectual-property and trade-secret protection; the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 requires re-training before a new application where the data requirement is not met. The operator's MDR notified body may control conformity with Section 2 only if its compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) was assessed in its notification. The result is a single procedure and a single CE marking. Finally, under Article 43(4) a substantial modification triggers a new conformity assessment, while changes to a continuously learning system that were pre-determined at the initial assessment and documented under point 2(f) of Annex IV do not constitute a substantial modification.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No, a biometric verification system whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be is not a prohibited practice, and it is not high-risk by virtue of the biometrics area of Annex III. On prohibition, none of the eight practices listed in Article 5(1) captures one-to-one verification: it is not a subliminal, manipulative or deceptive technique (point (a)), nor exploitation of vulnerabilities of age, disability or a specific social or economic situation (point (b)), nor social scoring leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or disproportionate to the social behaviour (point (c)(i), (ii)), nor criminal-offence risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits (point (d)), nor the untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion inference in the workplace or education, biometric categorisation deducing race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation (points (e), (g)), nor the use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, which is confined to the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and missing persons, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety or of a terrorist attack, and the localisation or identification of a suspect for Annex II offences punishable by at least four years (point (h)(i), (iii)). Verification against a claimed identity is not remote biometric identification. On classification, Annex III, point 1(a) lists remote biometric identification systems but states expressly that this "shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be". The exclusion is built into the listed use case itself, so the system is outside Article 6(2) and you never reach the Article 6(3) derogation or its conditions. Points 1(b) (biometric categorisation by sensitive or protected attributes) and 1(c) (emotion recognition) are likewise not engaged. Three qualifications govern that conclusion. First, the exclusion depends on "sole purpose": if the system also performs one-to-many identification, categorisation or emotion inference, or is used to identify persons who have not asserted an identity, it falls back within Annex III, point 1. Second, the exclusion operates only within the biometrics area; if the verification component is deployed inside another Annex III area, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, or administration of justice and democratic processes, that listed use case must be assessed on its own terms. Third, the Annex III route is distinct from the Annex I product route: under Article 6(1) the system is high-risk irrespective of Annex III if it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. The Annex III, point 1 chapeau also confirms that the use must in any event be permitted under relevant Union or national law, so the underlying processing of biometric data remains subject to the applicable data protection regime. If the system interacts directly with natural persons, Article 50(1) still applies: as provider the operator must ensure it is designed and developed so that the persons concerned are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances and context of use; this does not apply to systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties, unless they are available to the public to report a criminal offence. Under Article 50(5) that information must be given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of the first interaction and must conform to applicable accessibility requirements, and under Article 50(6) it is without prejudice to other transparency obligations in Union or national law. Article 50(3) does not bite, since verification is neither emotion recognition nor biometric categorisation.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Human oversight measures are governed by Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Article 14(1) requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use. Article 14(2) sets the objective of that oversight: to prevent or minimise the risks to health, safety or fundamental rights that may emerge when the system is used in accordance with its intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, in particular where such risks persist despite the other requirements of that Section. Under Article 14(3), the oversight measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, and are ensured through either or both of two types of measures: (a) measures identified and built into the system by the provider before placing on the market or putting into service, when technically feasible; and (b) measures identified by the provider before placing on the market or putting into service that are appropriate to be implemented by the deployer. Article 14(4) requires the system to be provided to the deployer so that the natural persons assigned oversight are enabled, as appropriate and proportionate: (a) to properly understand the relevant capacities and limitations of the system and duly monitor its operation, including detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance; (b) to remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output (automation bias), in particular where the system provides information or recommendations for decisions taken by natural persons; (c) to correctly interpret the system's output, taking into account the interpretation tools and methods available; (d) to decide, in any particular situation, not to use the system or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse its output; and (e) to intervene in the operation of the system or interrupt it through a 'stop' button or similar procedure that allows the system to come to a halt in a safe state. Article 14(5) adds a specific rule for the remote biometric identification systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III: no action or decision may be taken by the deployer on the basis of the identification resulting from the system unless that identification has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority. That two-person verification requirement does not apply to high-risk AI systems used for the purposes of law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum where Union or national law considers its application to be disproportionate.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non‑compliance with the prohibited AI practices laid down in Article 5 attracts the Regulation's highest penalty tier: administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). This ceiling applies to any of the eight prohibitions in Article 5(1), subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques; exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation; social scoring producing detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or disproportionate to the social behaviour; criminal‑risk prediction based solely on profiling or personality traits; untargeted scraping of facial images to build facial‑recognition databases; emotion inference in the workplace and in education; biometric categorisation deducing sensitive attributes; and real‑time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement outside the exhaustive derogations. Two qualifications attach to that ceiling. First, where the offender is an SME, including a start‑up, the fine is capped at the lower of the percentage and the fixed amount, rather than the higher (Article 99(6)). Second, the amount actually imposed must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive and must take into account the interests of small‑scale providers and their economic viability (Article 99(1)); in each individual case regard must be had to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences, whether other authorities have already fined the same operator for the same infringement, whether other authorities have already fined the operator for infringements of other Union or national law arising from the same activity, the size, annual turnover and market share of the operator, any other aggravating or mitigating factor such as financial benefits gained or losses avoided, the degree of cooperation with national competent authorities, the degree of responsibility of the operator taking into account the technical and organisational measures it implemented, the manner in which the infringement became known to the authorities and in particular whether the operator notified it, the intentional or negligent character of the infringement, and any action taken to mitigate the harm suffered by affected persons (Article 99(7)). The Article 99(3) tier is distinct from and higher than the EUR 15 000 000 / 3 % tier for the closed list of operator and notified‑body duties (Articles 16, 22, 23, 24, 26, 31, 33(1), (3) and (4), 34 and 50), which is expressly stated to apply to provisions "other than those laid down in Article 5", and from the EUR 7 500 000 / 1 % tier for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities (Article 99(4) and (5)). Member States lay down the rules on penalties and ensure they are properly and effectively implemented, notifying them to the Commission (Article 99(1) and (2)); depending on the national legal system, fines may be imposed by national courts or other bodies, and their exercise is subject to appropriate procedural safeguards including effective judicial remedies and due process (Article 99(9) and (10)). Member States must also notify the Commission of those rules and measures on an annual basis, together with a report on the administrative fines issued that year and any related litigation or judicial proceedings (Article 99(11)).

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Article 1 sets out the Regulation's subject matter in two layers. Its stated purpose is to improve the functioning of the internal market and to promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and the fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation (Article 1(1)). To that end, the Regulation lays down: harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service and the use of AI systems in the Union; prohibitions of certain AI practices; specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems; harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems; harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models; rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement; and measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on SMEs, including start-ups (Article 1(2)(a), (g)).

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine on providers of general-purpose AI models, and in exercising it the Court may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed (Article 101(5)). "Unlimited jurisdiction" means the Court is not confined to reviewing the legality of the decision but may substitute its own assessment of the amount for the Commission's, including raising the fine above the level the Commission set, subject to the ceiling in Article 101(1) of 3 % of the provider's annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher. The fines so reviewable are those the Commission may impose where it finds that the provider intentionally or negligently infringed the relevant provisions of the Regulation, failed to comply with a request for a document or for information under Article 91 or supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, failed to comply with a measure requested under Article 93, or failed to make available to the Commission access to the general-purpose AI model or general-purpose AI model with systemic risk with a view to an evaluation pursuant to Article 92 (Article 101(1)(a), (d)). The Court's review extends to the fixing criteria the Commission must apply, the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, with due account of proportionality and appropriateness, and account taken of commitments made under Article 93(3) or in codes of practice under Article 56 (Article 101(1)), and to the requirement that fines be effective, proportionate and dissuasive (Article 101(3)). It also covers the procedural safeguard that, before adopting the decision, the Commission must communicate its preliminary findings to the provider and give it an opportunity to be heard (Article 101(2)), and the procedural arrangements laid down in the implementing acts adopted under Article 101(6).

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: A provider registering a high-risk AI system must enter the data listed in Section A of Annex VIII into the EU database, doing so itself or through its authorised representative before the system is placed on the market or put into service (Article 49(1); Article 71(2)). The required items are the thirteen members of that Section: the name, address and contact details of the provider; where the submission is made by another person on the provider's behalf, that person's name, address and contact details; the name, address and contact details of the authorised representative, where applicable; the AI system's trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability of the system; a description of the intended purpose of the AI system and of the components and functions supported through it; a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic; the status of the AI system (on the market, or in service; no longer placed on the market or in service; recalled); the type, number and expiry date of the certificate issued by the notified body and the name or identification number of that body, where applicable; a scanned copy of that certificate, where applicable; any Member States in which the system has been placed on the market, put into service or made available in the Union; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; electronic instructions for use; and, optionally, a URL for additional information (Annex VIII, points 1 to 13). Three qualifications attach to that list. The electronic instructions for use are not to be provided for high-risk systems in the areas of law enforcement or migration, asylum and border control management referred to in Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7 (Annex VIII, point 12); for those same systems the registration is made in a secure non-public section of the database and is limited to Section A, points 1 to 10, excluding points 6, 8 and 9, together with the specified points of Sections B and C of Annex VIII and points 1, 2, 3 and 5 of Annex IX (Article 49(4)). High-risk systems falling under point 2 of Annex III are excluded from EU-database registration altogether and are registered at national level instead (Article 49(1) and (5)). Where the provider has instead concluded under Article 6(3) that an Annex III system is not high-risk, it must still register itself and the system, and the corresponding data set is Section B of Annex VIII (Article 49(2); Article 6(4); Article 71(2)); Section C is populated by deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies (Article 49(3); Article 71(3)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).

Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Under Article 13(3), a provider of a high-risk AI system must accompany that system with instructions for use in an appropriate digital or other format, containing concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers (Article 13(2)), and covering at least the following categories. First, the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, of its authorised representative (Article 13(3)(a)). Second, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the system (Article 13(3)(b)), comprising each of the following sub-points: its intended purpose; the level of accuracy, including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15 against which the system has been tested and validated and which can be expected, together with any known or foreseeable circumstances that may impact that expected level; any known or foreseeable circumstance, related to use in accordance with the intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, which may lead to risks to health and safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2); where applicable, the technical capabilities and characteristics of the system to provide information relevant to explaining its output; when appropriate, its performance regarding specific persons or groups of persons on which the system is intended to be used; when appropriate, specifications for the input data, or other relevant information on the training, validation and testing data sets used, taking into account the intended purpose; and, where applicable, information enabling deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately. Third, the changes to the system and its performance that were pre-determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment, if any (Article 13(3)(c)). Fourth, the human oversight measures referred to in Article 14, including the technical measures put in place to facilitate deployers' interpretation of the system's outputs (Article 13(3)(d)). Fifth, the computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime of the system, and any necessary maintenance and care measures, including their frequency, to ensure proper functioning, including as regards software updates (Article 13(3)(e)). Sixth, where relevant, a description of the mechanisms included within the system that allow deployers to properly collect, store and interpret the logs in accordance with Article 12 (Article 13(3)(f)). These instructions are also the vehicle through which the provider discharges the information element of its risk management duty under Article 9(5)(c), and the declared accuracy metrics required by Article 15(3) must be stated in them.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both, including with the involvement of any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, such as civil society organisations and academia; a single code may cover one or more AI systems, taking into account the similarity of the intended purpose of the relevant systems (Article 95(3)). The bodies charged with encouraging and facilitating them are the AI Office and the Member States. Under Article 95(1) they must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, including related governance mechanisms, intended to foster the voluntary application to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems of some or all of the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, taking into account available technical solutions and industry best practices. Under Article 95(2) the AI Office and the Member States must also facilitate the drawing up of codes concerning the voluntary application, including by deployers, of specific requirements to all AI systems, on the basis of clear objectives and key performance indicators measuring their achievement, covering elements such as applicable elements of Union ethical guidelines for trustworthy AI; assessing and minimising the impact of AI systems on environmental sustainability, including energy-efficient programming and efficient design, training and use; promoting AI literacy, in particular of persons dealing with the development, operation and use of AI; facilitating inclusive and diverse design, including through inclusive and diverse development teams and the promotion of stakeholder participation; and assessing and preventing negative impact on vulnerable persons or groups, including as regards accessibility for persons with a disability, as well as on gender equality. When encouraging and facilitating the drawing up of codes of conduct, the AI Office and the Member States must take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups (Article 95(4)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1), a provider of a high-risk AI system must put in place a quality management system that ensures compliance with the Regulation and is documented in a systematic and orderly manner in the form of written policies, procedures and instructions, covering at least thirteen aspects: (a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for managing modifications to the high-risk AI system; (b) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for the design, design control and design verification of the system; (c) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for its development, quality control and quality assurance; (d) examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development, and the frequency with which they are to be carried out; (e) technical specifications, including standards, to be applied and, where harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all relevant requirements of Chapter III, Section 2, the means used to ensure compliance with those requirements; (f) systems and procedures for data management, including data acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention and any other data operation performed before and for the purpose of placing on the market or putting into service; (g) the risk management system referred to in Article 9; (h) the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system in accordance with Article 72; (i) procedures related to the reporting of a serious incident in accordance with Article 73; (j) the handling of communication with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities including those providing or supporting access to data, notified bodies, other operators, customers or other interested parties; (k) systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information; (l) resource management, including security-of-supply related measures; and (m) an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of management and other staff with regard to all of those aspects (Article 17(1)). Three qualifications complete the duty. Implementation of those aspects must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation, but providers must in any event respect the degree of rigour and the level of protection required to ensure their high-risk AI systems comply with the Regulation (Article 17(2)). Providers already subject to quality management system obligations or an equivalent function under relevant sectoral Union law may integrate the Article 17(1) aspects into that existing system rather than operating a parallel one (Article 17(3)). For providers that are financial institutions subject to internal governance, arrangements or processes requirements under Union financial services law, the obligation to put a quality management system in place is deemed fulfilled by complying with those internal governance rules, with the exception of points (g), (h) and (i), the risk management system, post-market monitoring and serious incident reporting, which remain owed in full; harmonised standards referred to in Article 40 are to be taken into account for that purpose (Article 17(4)). The post-market monitoring element must itself be established and documented proportionately to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the system, and must actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant performance data provided by deployers or from other sources (Article 72(1), (2)). Voluntary management-system standards such as ISO 42001 or ISO 9001 may support implementation but do not discharge these statutory elements.

Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h), and may be used only where and in so far as such use is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustively listed objectives. (i) the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons (Article 5(1)(h)(i)); (ii) the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack (Article 5(1)(h)(ii)); and (iii) the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of conducting a criminal investigation or prosecution or executing a criminal penalty, for offences referred to in Annex II (terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children and child sexual abuse material, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs, weapons or nuclear and radioactive materials, murder, kidnapping, rape, armed robbery, participation in a criminal organisation, environmental crime and the other offences listed there) and punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years (Article 5(1)(h)(iii); Annex II). Point (h) is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for processing of biometric data for purposes other than law enforcement. These objectives are not self-executing permissions. Under Article 5(2), use for any of those objectives may serve only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual, and must take into account (a) the nature of the situation giving rise to the possible use, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of the harm that would be caused if the system were not used, and (b) the consequences of the use for the rights and freedoms of all persons concerned, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of those consequences; it must also comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions under the authorising national law, in particular temporal, geographic and personal limitations. Article 5(2) further conditions authorisation on the law-enforcement authority having completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and having registered the system in the EU database under Article 49, save that in duly justified cases of urgency use may begin before registration provided registration is completed without undue delay. Article 5(3) requires prior authorisation by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority of the Member State whose decision is binding, granted upon reasoned request; in a duly justified situation of urgency use may be started without authorisation, which must then be requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours, and if that authorisation is refused the use must be stopped immediately and all data, results and output discarded and deleted. Article 5(4) requires notification of each use to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority, and Article 5(5) leaves it to Member States to decide whether, and to what extent, to authorise such use at all within the limits of Article 5(1)(h) and paragraphs (2) and (3). Non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibition attracts the highest penalty tier under Article 99(3).

Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure that the outputs of the system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2)). The duty attaches to the provider at the level of system design, not to the deployer's later publication choices, and applies irrespective of whether the system is high-risk. The technical solution used to achieve that marking must meet four cumulative quality criteria: it must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable. Those criteria are qualified by a feasibility standard, they apply as far as this is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of the various types of content, the costs of implementation, and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards (Article 50(2)). To the extent the information is provided to natural persons, it must be given in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure and must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). The marking obligation does not apply in three situations: to the extent the AI systems perform an assistive function for standard editing; to the extent they do not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof; and where the AI systems are authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (Article 50(2)). This obligation does not affect the requirements and obligations set out in Chapter III and is without prejudice to other transparency obligations laid down in Union or national law (Article 50(6)). Implementation is to be supported by codes of practice at Union level, which the AI Office encourages and facilitates and which the Commission may approve by implementing act under the Article 56(6) procedure; where the Commission deems a code inadequate, it may adopt an implementing act specifying common rules for implementing the detection and labelling obligations under the Article 98(2) examination procedure (Article 50(7)). Compliance with harmonised standards is therefore the practical route to demonstrating that a marking solution meets the state-of-the-art benchmark, but such standards and codes do not themselves displace the statutory criteria in Article 50(2).

Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The European Commission holds those powers exclusively, and it entrusts their implementation to the AI Office. Article 88(1) confers on the Commission exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, the obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models, including the Article 53(1) duties (technical documentation per Annex XI, downstream-provider information per Annex XII, a copyright policy, and a public training-content summary) and the additional Article 55(1) obligations of providers of models with systemic risk, exercised taking into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94. The same paragraph requires the Commission to entrust implementation of those tasks to the AI Office, without prejudice to the Commission's own powers of organisation and to the division of competences between the Member States and the Union based on the Treaties; the AI Office therefore acts as the operational arm, while the enforcement power remains the Commission's. This exclusivity displaces national market-surveillance competence over Chapter V duties, though it does not isolate the two levels: under Article 88(2), and without prejudice to Article 75(3), market surveillance authorities may request the Commission to exercise the powers laid down in that Section where necessary and proportionate to assist them in fulfilling their tasks under the Regulation, relevant in particular where a general-purpose AI model is integrated into an AI system falling within those authorities' competence under Article 74. Correspondingly, Article 53(3) obliges providers of general-purpose AI models to cooperate as necessary with both the Commission and the national competent authorities in the exercise of their respective competences and powers.

AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, matching the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states that the Commission entrusts implementation of these tasks to the AI Office, satisfying the substance of criterion 2.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Under Article 60(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, data collected and processed for the purpose of testing a high-risk AI system in real world conditions may be transferred to a third country only provided that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented. The Act imposes no separate AI-specific transfer mechanism and sets no additional AI-specific condition; the safeguard requirement is a renvoi to the transfer rules of Union law generally, in practice the EU data protection transfer regime (adequacy, appropriate safeguards such as standard contractual clauses or binding corporate rules, or a derogation), together with the heightened conditions applicable where special categories of personal data are involved, and any sectoral Union law governing the data in question. The safeguards must be both "appropriate" and "applicable", so the mechanism relied on must be one that is legally available for the transfer concerned and effective in the destination jurisdiction, and it must remain in place for the duration of the processing. That condition is not free-standing: Article 60(4) permits testing in real world conditions only where all of its conditions are cumulatively met, so a compliant transfer presupposes that the remainder of the limbs are also satisfied, a real-world testing plan drawn up and submitted to the market surveillance authority of the Member State of testing; approval of the testing and the plan by that authority (with tacit approval after 30 days where national law so provides, otherwise a subsisting authorisation requirement); registration of the testing with a Union-wide unique single identification number, in the public EU database with the information specified in Annex IX, or in the secure non-public section for Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 systems in law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, or in accordance with Article 49(5) for Annex III point 2 systems; establishment of the provider or prospective provider in the Union or appointment of a legal representative established in the Union; a testing duration no longer than necessary and in any event not exceeding six months, extendable once by a further six months with prior notification and explanation; appropriate protection of subjects belonging to vulnerable groups by reason of age or disability; information to cooperating deployers or prospective deployers on all aspects relevant to their decision to participate; informed consent of the subjects of testing, subject to the law enforcement carve-out where seeking consent would prevent the system from being tested, in which case the testing and its outcome must have no negative effect on the subjects and their personal data must be deleted after the test; effective oversight of the testing by the provider or prospective provider and the deployers or prospective deployers through adequately qualified persons with the necessary capacity, training and authority; and the capacity for the system's predictions, recommendations or decisions to be effectively reversed and disregarded. Two further constraints bear directly on data that has been transferred. Under Article 60(5), a subject may withdraw informed consent at any time without detriment or justification and may request the immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data, which must be honoured wherever the data has been transferred, with the withdrawal not affecting activities already carried out. And under Article 60(3), the transfer and the underlying testing remain without prejudice to any ethical review required by Union or national law.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the two conditions are alternatives, not cumulative. Article 51(1) states that a general-purpose AI model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk "if it meets any of the following conditions", so satisfying either one suffices. (a) it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks (Article 51(1)(a)); or. (b) on the basis of a decision of the Commission, taken ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those in point (a), having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII (Article 51(1)(b)). Within limb (a), Article 51(2) supplies a rebuttable presumption rather than a third condition: a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than 10²⁵. "High-impact capabilities" means capabilities that match or exceed the capabilities recorded in the most advanced general-purpose AI models (Article 3(64)), and "systemic risk" is a risk specific to such capabilities, having a significant impact on the Union market due to their reach, or due to actual or reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or society as a whole, that can be propagated at scale across the value chain (Article 3(65)). The compute threshold and the benchmarks and indicators are themselves adjustable: the Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts under Article 97 to amend the thresholds in Article 51(1) and (2) and to supplement benchmarks and indicators in light of evolving technological developments such as algorithmic improvements or increased hardware efficiency (Article 51(3)). Logically prior to either limb, the model must first qualify as a general-purpose AI model within Article 3(63), an AI model displaying significant generality and capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks, integrable into a variety of downstream systems or applications, excluding models used for research, development or prototyping activities before placing on the market. Once the classification is triggered by either limb, the provider owes the Article 55(1) obligations in addition to those in Articles 53 and 54: (a) model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing with a view to identifying and mitigating systemic risks; (b) assessment and mitigation of possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources, stemming from the development, placing on the market or use of the model; (c) keeping track of, documenting and reporting without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures; and (d) ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and for the physical infrastructure of the model. The classification also removes the free and open-source carve-out: the exemption from Article 53(1), points (a) and (b), does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2)).
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. An AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) is not automatically high-risk under the Annex I product route, because Article 6(1) makes classification conditional on both limbs being satisfied cumulatively: under point (a) the AI system must be intended to be used as a safety component of, or be itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and under point (b) that product must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that same Annex I legislation. Here only the first limb is met. Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices is Annex I, point 11, so a safety component of an MDR device satisfies Article 6(1)(a). But a Class I device that is neither sterile, nor with a measuring function, nor a reusable surgical instrument is precisely the residual Class I category for which the MDR conformity assessment route involves no notified body, the manufacturer self-declares conformity. Because no third-party conformity assessment is required for the product, Article 6(1)(b) fails, and the cumulative test in Article 6(1) is not fulfilled. The classification therefore turns on the sectoral conformity-assessment route applicable to the host product, not on the mere fact that the product falls within Annex I. Two qualifications preserve the analysis. First, the conclusion depends on the device genuinely remaining in that self-certified Class I sub-category: if the classification changes (for example, the AI functionality itself qualifies as software that is a device and drives a higher class, or the device becomes sterile, measuring or a reusable surgical instrument), notified body involvement is triggered and Article 6(1)(b) is satisfied, making the system high-risk. Second, escaping Article 6(1) does not exhaust the Act. Under Article 6(2), AI systems referred to in Annex III are high-risk in addition to those under paragraph 1, so the system must still be tested against the listed use cases across the eight areas of biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits (which includes, at point 5(d), systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls or to dispatch or prioritise the dispatching of emergency first response services, including medical aid, as well as emergency healthcare patient triage systems); law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes. A typical safety component embedded in a surgical instrument will not match any lettered use case, but the check is separate and must be made. If a listed use case is matched, the Article 6(3) derogation may still apply where the system poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and it performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case, save that a system performing profiling of natural persons is always high-risk. A provider relying on that derogation must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service under Article 6(4), is subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2), and must provide that documentation to national competent authorities on request. That derogation is available only on the Annex III route and has no counterpart for Article 6(1).

Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a lift can qualify as a high-risk AI system, but only through the Annex I product route in Article 6(1), and only where both of its cumulative conditions are met. The first condition, Article 6(1)(a), is satisfied because lifts and safety components for lifts are covered by Directive 2014/33/EU, which is listed in Annex I, point 4. The second condition, Article 6(1)(b), requires that the product whose safety component the AI system is, the lift, or the safety component itself where the AI system is itself the product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that Annex I legislation. Where the applicable lift conformity assessment procedure does not involve a third party, the system does not become high-risk on this route. Classification under Article 6(1) applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift or of the safety component. The derogation in Article 6(3) is not available here: it applies only by derogation from Article 6(2), that is, to systems classified as high-risk because they fall within the Annex III listed use cases, and its conditions, a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment absent proper human review, or performing a preparatory task to an Annex III assessment, and in all cases subject to the rule that profiling of natural persons always yields high-risk status, have no application to the Annex I product route. Correspondingly, the documentation and Article 49(2) registration duties in Article 6(4) are confined to providers asserting that an Annex III system is not high-risk. Where the AI system is high-risk on this basis, Article 43(3) governs conformity assessment for systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, which includes the lifts Directive: the provider follows the relevant conformity assessment procedure required under that act, the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 apply and form part of that assessment, and points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply. Notified bodies notified under the lifts Directive may control conformity with those Section 2 requirements provided their compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) has been assessed in the notification procedure under that act. Where the lifts Directive enables the manufacturer to opt out of third-party conformity assessment on the basis that it has applied all harmonised standards covering the relevant requirements, that option may be used only if the manufacturer has also applied the harmonised standards or, where applicable, the common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all Section 2 requirements. Under Article 43(4), a new conformity assessment is required upon substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer, while pre-determined changes documented under point 2(f) of Annex IV for systems that continue to learn after placing on the market do not constitute a substantial modification. The internal-control procedure of Annex VI referred to in Article 43(1) and (2) is reserved for Annex III systems and is therefore not the route for a lift safety component.

Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: The two duties are cumulative, not alternative, and both fall on the provider. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation must immediately take the necessary corrective actions, bringing the system into conformity, withdrawing it, disabling it, or recalling it, as appropriate, and must inform the distributors of the system concerned and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers. Under Article 20(2), where that high-risk AI system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, the provider must immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the market surveillance authorities competent for the system concerned and, where applicable, the notified body that issued a certificate for it under Article 44, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken. The investigation duty is therefore the provider's own and arises on awareness of the risk; it is not deferred until an authority acts. The operator's alternative reading is incorrect. The market surveillance authority's role under Article 79(2) is a separate evaluation of the system's compliance with all requirements and obligations of the Regulation, triggered where it has sufficient reason to consider that the system presents a risk under Article 79(1); on finding non-compliance it must, without undue delay, require the operator to take appropriate corrective action, withdraw or recall the system within a prescribed period and in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period set by the relevant Union harmonisation legislation, informing the relevant notified body, with Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 applying to those measures. That authority-side evaluation runs in parallel with, and does not displace, the provider's Article 20 duties; the operator must cooperate as necessary with the authority and with the national public authorities or bodies referred to in Article 77(1), must ensure that all appropriate corrective action is taken in respect of all the systems concerned that it has made available on the Union market (Article 79(4)), and faces provisional prohibition, restriction, withdrawal or recall measures if it fails to take adequate corrective action in the period set (Article 79(5)). Where the risk materialises as a serious incident, the provider additionally reports under Article 73(1) within the applicable deadline and, following that report, must without delay perform the necessary investigations into the incident and the system, including a risk assessment and corrective action, cooperating with the competent authorities and any relevant notified body, and must not conduct any investigation involving alteration of the system in a way that may affect a subsequent evaluation of the incident's causes before informing the competent authorities of such action (Article 73(6)).
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority

The answer clearly assigns the duty to investigate causes to the provider under Article 20(2), stating it arises upon awareness of the risk.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate, the duty is real and expressly stated. Article 24(3) requires distributors to ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the compliance of the system with the requirements set out in Section 2. The "where applicable" qualifier is what answers the operator's software objection: the duty bites only where such conditions actually exist, but it is far from theoretical, because high-risk AI systems are frequently supplied embedded in or as a safety component of a physical product, or delivered on physical media, dedicated hardware or pre-configured devices, and handling in that state can degrade calibration, sensor integrity, logging capability or the accompanying documentation. The obligation does not stand alone. Before making a high-risk AI system available on the market, Article 24(1) requires the operator to verify that it bears the required CE marking, that it is accompanied by a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 and the instructions for use, and that the provider and the importer, as applicable, have complied with their respective obligations under Article 16, points (b) and (c), and Article 23(3). Under Article 24(2), where you consider or have reason to consider, on the basis of information in the operator's possession, that the system is not in conformity with the Section 2 requirements, the operator must not make it available until it has been brought into conformity, and where it presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) the operator must inform the provider or the importer accordingly. If the non-conformity concerns a system you have already made available, Article 24(4) requires the operator to take the corrective actions necessary to bring it into conformity, to withdraw or recall it, or to ensure that the provider, importer or other relevant operator takes those actions, and where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), to immediately inform the provider or importer and the competent authorities, giving details of the non-compliance and of any corrective actions taken. Article 24(5) obliges you, upon a reasoned request from a relevant competent authority, to provide all information and documentation regarding the operator's actions under paragraphs 1 to 4 necessary to demonstrate the system's conformity with the Section 2 requirements, and Article 24(6) requires the operator to cooperate with the competent authorities in any action they take in relation to a high-risk AI system you have made available, in particular to reduce or mitigate the risk it poses.

Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: The system described is not among the practices prohibited under Article 5 (social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, manipulative or exploitative techniques, and the other exhaustively-listed bans). Whether it is high-risk turns on Article 6: it is high-risk only if it is a safety component of a product regulated under Annex I (for example a medical device under the MDR or IVDR) or falls within one of the Annex III use cases. Otherwise it is limited- or minimal-risk, subject mainly to the Article 50 transparency duties where it interacts directly with people.

Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)

The answer does not address that using AI in a drone to identify people in public constitutes remote biometric identification, which is high-risk under Annex III(1)(a); it omits this specific application and its consequences.

The answer does not specifically address toy drones used for other applications, nor does it assess such uses against Annex III or Article 6(1) criteria.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No. You cannot simply proceed with the new use, and yes, the operator must keep the logs. On the first point, Article 26(1) obliges deployers to take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure they use high-risk AI systems in accordance with the instructions for use accompanying the system. A use that the operator's own analysis characterises as outside the intended use is, by definition, outside those instructions, so deploying it breaches Article 26(1) irrespective of how benign the new use is. The operator's legal team's conclusion answers a different question from the one that matters here: Article 6 fixes the system's classification by reference to the intended purpose declared by the provider, either as a safety component of, or as, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation exhaustively listed in Annex I.1 to I.20 and subject to third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)), or as one of the lettered use-cases under the eight areas of Annex III (Article 6(2)). The system you deployed is already high-risk on one of those routes; the fact that a further, additional use would not on its own engage Annex I or Annex III does not declassify the system, and a deployer has no power to re-run the classification. Nor is the Article 6(3) derogation available to you: it applies only to the Annex III route, only where the system poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and only where one of its four conditions is met, a narrow procedural task (Article 6(3)(a)), improving the result of a previously completed human activity (point (b)), detecting decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment absent proper human review (point (c)), or performing a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case (point (d)), with the override that a system performing profiling of natural persons is always high-risk. That derogation is a provider self-assessment documented before the system is placed on the market, not a deployer-side release valve. There is a second exposure. Under Article 25(1)(b) a deployer that makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, in such a way that it remains high-risk under Article 6, is itself considered a provider and assumes the full Article 16 provider obligations; Article 25(1)(c) does the same where the intended purpose of a system not previously classified as high-risk is modified so that it becomes high-risk, and Article 25(1)(a) where a party puts its own name or trademark on the system. If the operator's new use is implemented by changing the system's intended purpose or by modifying the system itself, you risk stepping into provider status, which carries the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, including the Article 9 risk-management system covering risks emerging under reasonably foreseeable misuse, Article 10 data governance, Article 11 technical documentation per Annex IV, Article 15 accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, plus Article 43 conformity assessment, the Article 47 EU declaration of conformity, CE marking and registration. Where Article 25(1) is triggered, the initial provider ceases to be the provider of that system and must cooperate and make available the necessary information and reasonably expected technical access and assistance, in particular for the conformity assessment, unless it clearly specified that its system is not to be changed into a high-risk AI system. The correct route is therefore to have the provider extend the declared intended purpose and the instructions for use, rather than to deploy off-label on the strength of an internal risk view. On logging, Article 26(6) requires you as deployer to keep the logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system, to the extent such logs are under the operator's control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and of at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law, in particular Union law on personal data protection, provides otherwise. That duty attaches to the high-risk AI system, not to the particular use to which the operator puts it, so it continues to apply to operation under the new use; and since the new use is off-label, the logs are precisely what a market surveillance authority will ask for. The only qualification in Article 26 is for deployers that are financial institutions subject to Union financial-services law requirements on internal governance, arrangements or processes: they are deemed to fulfil the Article 26(6) log-retention obligation, as well as the Article 26(5) monitoring obligation, by complying with those internal governance rules. Alongside retention, Article 26(5) requires the operator to monitor operation on the basis of the instructions for use and to inform the provider of serious incidents, and, where the system is used in the workplace, Article 26(7) requires the operator to inform workers' representatives and the affected workers before putting the system into service.

Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
