rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes. AI software that supports clinicians in deciding the best treatment for a patient is potentially high-risk, and the route that captures it is Article 6(1) read with Annex I, not Annex III. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk, irrespective of whether it is placed on the market or put into service independently of a product, where both conditions are met: (a) it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; and (b) that product, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service under that Annex I legislation. Clinical decision-support software of this kind is normally software qualifying as a medical device, or as an in vitro diagnostic device where the recommendation is driven by examination of specimens, under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (Annex I, point 11) or Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (Annex I, point 12). Because software that provides information used to take decisions for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes is classified above the self-certification floor under those regimes, it requires notified-body involvement, so condition (b) is satisfied and the system is high-risk. Conformity assessment then runs through the MDR/IVDR notified-body procedure, producing a single CE marking, and the Article 9 risk-management and Article 10 data-governance requirements map onto existing ISO 14971 and ISO 13485 practice. Annex III is not the operative hook for treatment recommendation as such. Its healthcare-adjacent entries are narrower: Annex III, point 5(a) covers AI used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them; point 5(c) covers risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance; and point 5(d) covers evaluation and classification of emergency calls and the dispatching or prioritisation of emergency first response services, including emergency healthcare patient triage systems. A clinician-facing treatment adviser would fall under Annex III only if it were in fact performing one of those listed functions, in which case it would be high-risk under Article 6(2). The distinction matters for the derogation: the Article 6(3) filter, narrow procedural task (point (a)), improving the result of a previously completed human activity (point (b)), detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment absent proper human review (point (c)), or performing a preparatory task to an Annex III assessment (point (d)), each conditional on the system not posing a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and in all cases disapplied where the system performs profiling of natural persons, applies only by derogation from paragraph 2, i.e. only to Annex III systems. It is therefore unavailable to a medical-device system that is high-risk via Article 6(1), which cannot be argued down on the basis that the clinician retains the final call. Article 50 adds nothing to classification here; at most Article 50(1) would require disclosure of the AI nature of the system to any natural person it interacts with directly, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the context of use. The one condition left to resolve on the facts is the device qualification and risk class of the specific software under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 or (EU) 2017/746; if it were genuinely outside those regimes or subject only to self-assessment, Article 6(1)(b) would not be met and the system would not be high-risk on the Annex I route.

Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Four of the five must be disclosed; the fifth must not. Date of release, yes. Number of parameters, yes. How the model interacts with hardware, yes. Licence, yes. Samples of outlier training data, no. The governing duty is Article 53(1)(b): a GPAI provider must draw up, keep up to date and make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems who intend to integrate the model, which must (i) enable those providers to understand the model's capabilities and limitations and to comply with their own obligations under the Regulation, and (ii) contain at a minimum the elements set out in Annex XII. Annex XII, point 1, requires a general description of the model comprising the tasks it is intended to perform and the type and nature of AI systems into which it can be integrated; the acceptable use policies applicable; the date of release and methods of distribution; how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself, where applicable; the versions of relevant software related to its use, where applicable; the architecture and number of parameters; the modality and format of inputs and outputs; and the licence for the model. Point 2 adds the technical means required for integration into AI systems, the modality and format of inputs and outputs and their maximum size (such as context window length), and information on the data used for training, testing and validation where applicable, including the type and provenance of the data and the curation methodologies. Release date, parameter count, hardware/software interaction (subject to its "where applicable" qualifier) and licence therefore all sit squarely in Annex XII, point 1. Outlier data samples do not: the training-data element of Annex XII, point 2 is descriptive, type, provenance and curation methodology, and nowhere requires the handover of data specimens, outliers or otherwise. Nor does the separate Article 53(1)(d) duty change this, since that is a publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of training content drawn up according to the AI Office template, not a disclosure of data samples to downstream providers. Two qualifiers bound the four affirmative answers. First, Article 53(1)(b) applies without prejudice to the need to observe and protect intellectual property rights and confidential business information or trade secrets under Union and national law, and anything obtained under trade secrets included, is handled under the confidentiality regime of Article 78 by virtue of Article 53(7). Second, under Article 53(2) the Article 53(1)(b) obligation does not apply at all to a model released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution and whose parameters, including the weights, the information on model architecture and the information on model usage, are publicly available; that exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk within the meaning of Article 51, for which the full Article 53(1) set plus the Article 55(1) obligations apply regardless of licence.

Architecture and number of parameters - Yes

Samples of outlier training data - No

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: Annex III lists eight areas of high-risk use cases, and an AI system is high-risk under Article 6(2) only where it falls within one of the lettered use-cases under those headings: biometrics (in so far as their use is permitted under Union or national law); critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits; law enforcement (in so far as permitted); migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III, points 1 to 8). No, healthcare decision-making is not one of the areas, there is no Annex III heading for health or clinical decision-making as such. Health-related uses reach high-risk status only through two other routes. First, within Annex III point 5 (access to essential private and public services and benefits), the listed use-cases capture: systems used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them (Annex III, point 5(a)); risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons for life and health insurance (Annex III, point 5(c)); and evaluation and classification of emergency calls, or dispatching and priority-setting for emergency first response services including medical aid, as well as emergency healthcare patient triage systems (Annex III, point 5(d)). Second, clinical AI is more commonly high-risk under the Annex I product route: a system that is itself a medical device or in vitro diagnostic device, or a safety component of one, under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 or Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (Annex I, points 11 and 12), is high-risk where that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation (Article 6(1)(a) and (b)). Two qualifications complete the picture. An Annex III system escapes high-risk classification under the Article 6(3) derogation where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and it performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or performs a preparatory task, but it is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons (Article 6(3)). Conversely, the Commission may by delegated act add or modify use-cases in Annex III only where both conditions are met cumulatively: the systems are intended to be used in an area already listed in Annex III, and they pose a risk of harm to health and safety or an adverse impact on fundamental rights equivalent to or greater than that of the systems already listed (Article 7(1)(a) and (b)). General clinical decision support therefore cannot be added as a free-standing health area; it would have to fit an existing Annex III area or qualify under Article 6(1).

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No, guardrails alone cannot move a system out of the high-risk class, whereas a genuine change to its capabilities and intended purpose can, because classification under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 turns on intended purpose and listed use-case, not on the strength of the controls wrapped around the system. Two further framing points matter: the Act as adopted contains no "moderate risk" class that a system can be downgraded into; outside the prohibited practices and the high-risk class, a system is either subject only to the actor-specific transparency duties of Article 50 (AI-interaction disclosure by providers, synthetic-content marking, emotion-recognition and biometric-categorisation notification, deepfake and public-interest-text labelling by deployers, with the law-enforcement, artistic-work and editorial-responsibility carve-outs) or to no Chapter III duties at all. On guardrails: Article 8(1) requires a high-risk system to meet the Chapter III Section 2 requirements taking into account its intended purpose and the state of the art, with the Article 9 risk-management system taken into account in ensuring that compliance, mitigation is therefore a consequence of high-risk status, not an escape from it. Article 9 expressly contemplates identifying foreseeable risks, estimating risks arising under reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluating post-market data and adopting targeted risk-control measures; a system that has done all of this remains high-risk with a reduced residual risk. Article 25(1)(b) confirms the direction of travel: a substantial modification to a high-risk system is addressed on the assumption that it "remains a high-risk AI system pursuant to Article 6", and the effect is to make the modifier a provider bearing the Article 16 obligations, not to relieve anyone of them. Guardrails instead feed the documentation chain, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance under Article 13(3)(b), the accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels and the circumstances affecting them under Article 13(3)(b)(ii), the known or foreseeable circumstances arising in intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse that may lead to risks under Article 13(3)(b)(iii), the pre-determined changes to the system and its performance under Article 13(3)(c), and the human-oversight measures under Article 13(3)(d). The only place where the effectiveness of mitigation and redress measures formally bears on high-risk status is Article 7(2)(k)(i)-(ii), and that is a criterion for the Commission's own delegated-act assessment under Article 7(1)(b) and for removal from Annex III under Article 7(3), exercised through the Article 97 delegation procedure, it is not a self-assessment lever available to a provider or deployer. On capabilities and intended purpose: this is the operative variable. Annex III makes a system high-risk only where it falls within one of the lettered use-cases under the eight areas (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes), so narrowing the declared intended purpose and removing the agent's capability to perform that listed use-case, not merely instructing it not to, can place the system outside the class prospectively. Article 25(1)(c) states the mirror image expressly: modifying the intended purpose of a system not classified as high-risk so that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 makes the modifier a provider subject to Article 16, which confirms that intended purpose is the classification determinant. For this to work the restriction must be real and reflected in the technical design, the declared intended purpose, the instructions for use and the input-data specifications under Article 13(3)(b)(i) and (vi), and in the Article 9 assessment of reasonably foreseeable misuse: if the agentic system retains the technical capability and the deployment context in which the Annex III use-case is a reasonably foreseeable use, a paper restriction will not hold. A reclassification is also prospective only, it does not retroactively cure the obligations that applied while the system was placed on the market as high-risk, including the Article 12 logging and Article 19 and Article 26(6) six-month minimum retention duties, the Article 47 declaration of conformity retained for ten years, and the Article 49 registration. For an agentic system built on a general-purpose AI model, note separately that Article 51 systemic-risk classification follows high-impact capabilities, presumed above 10^25 FLOPs cumulative training compute under Article 51(2) or designated by the Commission under Article 51(1)(b) on the Annex XIII criteria. Guardrails at the system layer do not affect that model-level designation either; only the model's actual capabilities, compute and reach do.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the use is allowed, and yes, the artificial nature must be disclosed; the lighter, "does-not-hamper-enjoyment" form of disclosure does not apply to an educational dermatology illustration, and the law-enforcement carve-out plainly does not. Nothing in the Regulation prohibits generating synthetic clinical images for teaching. Article 5 lists exhaustively the prohibited practices, and none is engaged: the images are not subliminal or deceptive techniques distorting behaviour to cause significant harm, not exploitation of vulnerability, not social scoring, not criminal-risk profiling, not untargeted facial scraping, not emotion inference in an educational institution, not biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, and not real-time remote biometric identification (Article 5(1)). Nor is the use high-risk: the education area of Annex III covers only the listed use-cases, determining admission or assignment to institutions, evaluating learning outcomes including those steering the learning process, assessing the appropriate level of education a person will receive or can access, and monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour during tests (Annex III, point 3), and generating illustrative teaching material is none of them, so the Chapter III requirements and the Article 27 fundamental-rights impact assessment are not triggered. The applicable duty is the transparency duty in Article 50. As deployer of an AI system generating image content constituting a deep fake, the university must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4), first subparagraph). That paragraph admits only two qualifications for image, audio and video deep fakes: the obligation does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute a criminal offence; and where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, the disclosure is limited to disclosing the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work (Article 50(4), second and third subparagraphs). The criminal-law exemption is confined to law-enforcement purposes and has no bearing on university teaching. The attenuated regime is reserved for works whose artificiality is evident from their expressive character; a synthetic image presented to medical students as a faithful depiction of how a dermatological condition actually appears is offered for its truth value, not as fiction or creative expression, and an "analogous work" must be analogous to the artistic, creative, satirical and fictional categories listed, an educational or illustrative purpose is not such an analogue. The pedagogical stakes point the same way: students are meant to rely on the morphology shown, so the fact that it is synthetic rather than a photograph of a real presentation is precisely the information they need. Full disclosure under the first subparagraph therefore applies, and the third and fourth subparagraphs' separate regime for artificially generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, with its exemptions for authorised criminal-law use and for content that has undergone human review or editorial control where a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility, is not in play here; in particular, academic review of the images by a clinician does not excuse deep-fake disclosure, since that exemption attaches only to the text duty. Practically, the disclosure must be given to the exposed persons in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first exposure, and must comply with the applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)), a caption, watermark or slide legend identifying the image as AI-generated, or an equivalent statement made at the start of the teaching material, satisfies this. Separately, and as a duty of the provider rather than of the university, the provider of the generative system must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, using effective, interoperable, robust and reliable technical solutions, save to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law for criminal-law purposes (Article 50(2)). If the university fine-tunes or otherwise supplies such a system under its own name, it would assume those provider obligations (Article 25(1)). Finally, Article 50 applies without prejudice to the other requirements and obligations of the Regulation and to other Union or national law (Article 50(6)), so obligations arising outside the AI Act, data-protection rules where a real patient's likeness underlies the synthesis, and professional or academic-integrity standards for teaching material, remain to be observed independently.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On the facts as described, this system is not high-risk, and it is not a prohibited practice either; the retailer's self-classification overstates its legal position. The social-scoring prohibition in Article 5(1)(c) does not bite. It requires evaluation or classification of natural persons over a certain period of time on the basis of their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, with the resulting social score leading to either or both of (i) detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated or collected, or (ii) detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity. A tool confined to the current cart and the current checkout event builds no persistent score over time and no personality profile; the only consequence, an optional manual bag check at the same till by store staff, arises in the very context in which the data was generated, so limb (i) fails, and a bag check is neither unjustified nor disproportionate to a checkout anomaly, so limb (ii) fails. Recital 31 confirms that the target is scoring across multiple contexts and data points, which is absent here. Article 5(1)(d) likewise does not apply. It prohibits AI systems making risk assessments of natural persons to assess or predict the risk of committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics, and it expressly does not apply to systems supporting the human assessment of a person's involvement in criminal activity where that assessment is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity. Checkout and cart anomalies are objective, verifiable transaction facts, the output is a flag for a human staff decision, and no profiling or trait inference occurs, so the practice falls outside the prohibition and, in any event, within its carve-out. Nor does any high-risk route open: there are no biometrics engaging the Annex III biometrics area, and the Annex III law-enforcement area concerns use by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities in criminal proceedings, which a private retailer conducting voluntary bag checks is not; resemblance to policing is not a listed use-case. The classification would change only if the tool were re-engineered to accumulate per-customer histories, infer traits, or predict propensity to offend, which would reopen Article 5(1)(c) and (d). Article 5(8) preserves prohibitions arising under other Union law, notably data-protection rules.

Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No. Applying harmonised standards instead of a notified body does not release you from Chapter III, Section 2, it is precisely the condition on which that opt‑out is made available. For a high‑risk AI system that is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Section A of Annex I, Article 43(3) states that the requirements set out in Section 2 of Chapter III shall apply to that system and shall be part of the sectoral assessment. The final subparagraph of Article 43(3) then deals expressly with the operator's situation: where a Section A legal act enables the product manufacturer to opt out of a third‑party conformity assessment on condition that it has applied all harmonised standards covering all the relevant requirements, the manufacturer may use that option only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, the common specifications referred to in Article 41, covering all requirements set out in Section 2 of this Chapter. So the opt‑out is lawful only where the operator's Section 2 compliance is itself demonstrated through harmonised standards or common specifications covering all of those requirements; if any Section 2 requirement is not so covered, the opt‑out is unavailable to you and the relevant sectoral third‑party procedure must be followed, in which case Points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of Point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply, and the notified body notified under the sectoral act may control conformity with Section 2 where its compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) was assessed in its notification. Note also that the internal‑control route of Annex VI under Article 43(1) is not open to you: it is reserved for high‑risk systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, not for the Annex I product route. Finally, under Article 43(4) any substantial modification triggers a fresh conformity assessment, and pre‑determined changes documented at the initial assessment under point 2(f) of Annex IV do not count as such. In short, Section 2 is not skippable, it is the substance the operator must have satisfied, and evidenced through those standards, in order to have taken the opt‑out at all.
